---
title: "Week 11 — Consuming APIs & Data Endpoints"
---

> The client side of client–server. This module teaches how a Streamlit app talks to a server over HTTP — REST basics, requests, JSON — through worked examples that consume ready-made endpoints, setting up the model-serving work to come.

## 📖 Background & Motivation

Until now, every app has been self-contained: the data and any computation live inside the Streamlit script. Real data-science applications rarely work that way. Data lives behind APIs, and models run on servers — separate processes, often on separate machines — that the front-end talks to over HTTP. Separating the *client* (the app the user sees) from the *server* (where data and models live) is what lets a visualization scale, stay secure, and reuse a model across many front-ends.

This week is deliberately client-only: we learn the request/response pattern by *consuming* endpoints that already exist, so the networking concepts land before we add the complexity of writing a server. You will hit public REST APIs and a small provided course endpoint, parse JSON responses into pandas, handle errors and latency gracefully, and visualize what comes back inside Streamlit. Next week (12) you build the server side; the week after (13) you visualize live model output. Think of these three weeks as one arc: **consume → serve → visualize.**

---

## 🔎 Learning Objectives

- Explain the client–server model and the structure of an HTTP request/response.
- Call REST APIs from Python with `requests` and parse JSON into pandas.
- Handle errors, status codes, and latency gracefully in a Streamlit client.
- Check a response past its status code — content type and shape — and explain why a 200 is not a promise.
- Send an authenticated request, keeping the key out of the code.
- Visualize data fetched live from an endpoint, with caching.

## 📚 Readings & Resources

- [MDN — An overview of HTTP](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Overview) — request/response basics.
- [Requests — quickstart](https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user/quickstart/).
- [What is a REST API?](https://www.redhat.com/en/topics/api/what-is-a-rest-api) — conceptual.
- [Streamlit — caching data](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/concepts/architecture/caching) — caching API calls.

**Endpoints for practice — all public, no key, no account:**

- [USGS earthquakes](https://earthquake.usgs.gov/fdsnws/event/1/) — GeoJSON, with `minmagnitude`, `starttime` and `bbox` as query parameters. The main example this week.
- [Open-Meteo](https://open-meteo.com/) — free weather API, hourly time series.
- [Frankfurter](https://frankfurter.dev/) — exchange rates, latest and by date range.
- `course_endpoint.py` in this week's materials — **you run it yourself**, in a second terminal. There is no shared server.

::: {.callout-warning title="Two APIs that used to be here"}
[REST Countries](https://restcountries.com/) and the [Census ACS
API](https://api.census.gov/) were both keyless and are no longer usable for
this course. REST Countries was taken down and answers every request with a
deprecation notice — at HTTP 200, as valid JSON, so `raise_for_status()`
passes and the failure surfaces later as a type error. Census now answers
without a key by returning an HTML page, also at 200.

Neither is a dead link; both are live endpoints that lie. Part B of the Block 2
demo uses them as worked examples, which is the only reason they are still
mentioned.
:::

## 🛠️ Setup Checklist

Make sure your environment includes:

```bash
pip install requests pandas matplotlib streamlit fastapi uvicorn scikit-learn
```

`requests`, `pandas` and `matplotlib` are for the client work. `fastapi`,
`uvicorn` and `scikit-learn` are for `course_endpoint.py`, the small server you
run yourself in Block 2 — and they are the same three you will need in Week 12,
when you write the server instead of just starting it.

Before class, confirm two things:

```bash
# 1. you can reach a public endpoint
python -c "import requests; print(requests.get('https://earthquake.usgs.gov/fdsnws/event/1/query?format=geojson&limit=1', timeout=20).status_code)"

# 2. you can start the course endpoint (Ctrl-C to stop it again)
uvicorn course_endpoint:app --port 8001
```

Part D of the demo calls two model APIs and needs `pip install anthropic openai`
plus a key for each. It is an instructor demo — the cells skip themselves when a
key is absent, so nothing below depends on it.

::: {.callout-important title="One trap worth knowing before you hit it"}
If an SDK call fails with `APIConnectionError: Connection error.` while plain
`requests` calls work, it is not your network. Anaconda ships `Brotli 1.0.9`,
and both vendors' SDKs use an HTTP layer that calls a newer Brotli API, so the
*response* fails to decompress — and the error it raises names the wrong cause
entirely. Fix:

```bash
pip install -U Brotli
```
:::

## 🧭 Session Outline (2.5 hours)

> Single 2.5-hour block, 6:10-8:40 PM. Tooling week — the guided demo is the longest block.

### Block 1 — Concepts & Theory (~45 min, PowerPoint)

1. Client vs. server: why we separate them (8 min)
2. Anatomy of an HTTP request: method, URL, params, headers, status codes (10 min)
3. Finding the table inside nested JSON (6 min)
4. When a 200 is not a success: the three checks, and why versioning is the defence (12 min)
5. Keys, headers and what a model call costs (9 min)

### Block 2 — Guided Demonstration (~70 min, live coding)

1. **A — USGS earthquakes:** request → check → parse → DataFrame, and query parameters as the interface (18 min)
2. **B — when a 200 is not a success:** three live APIs failing three different ways, and the three checks that catch them (16 min)
3. **C — the course endpoint:** start your own server, and a deliberate 404 (10 min)
4. **D — APIs that need a key:** headers and auth, the same call to two vendors, and what tokens, latency and cost look like side by side. Instructor demo (18 min)
5. **E — into Streamlit:** caching, and killing the server to watch the client degrade (8 min)

### ☕ Break (~15 min)

### Block 3 — Hands-On Activity (~50 min, on your own after class)

1. Pick an API, fetch and parse it in the notebook, and check the response past its status (15 min)
2. Move the call into a Streamlit client: one widget on a **request parameter**, cached (20 min)
3. Break it on purpose and handle the failure gracefully (15 min)

Students who use the course endpoint run their own copy:
`uvicorn course_endpoint:app --port 8001`, in a second terminal.

### Block 4 — Wrap-Up & Homework Preview (~10 min)

1. Share apps; discuss latency/error handling (6 min)
2. Preview homework and Week 12 (you'll build the server next) (4 min)

## 💻 Notebook / App Snippets

### Open-Meteo — parallel arrays into a tidy frame

```python
import requests, pandas as pd

r = requests.get(
    "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast",
    params={"latitude": 38.9, "longitude": -77.0, "hourly": "temperature_2m"},
    timeout=10,
)
r.raise_for_status()
data = r.json()["hourly"]
df = pd.DataFrame({"time": pd.to_datetime(data["time"]), "temp": data["temperature_2m"]})
```

### Three checks, not one

`raise_for_status()` checks the status. Against an API you do not control that
is the weakest of the three things worth checking, because a 200 only means the
server chose to answer.

```python
import streamlit as st, requests

@st.cache_data(ttl=300)
def get_json(url, params=None, timeout=20, expect=dict):
    r = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=timeout)
    r.raise_for_status()                                   # 1. status

    ctype = r.headers.get("content-type", "")
    if "json" not in ctype:                                # 2. content type
        raise ValueError(f"expected JSON, got {ctype!r}: {r.text[:120]}")

    payload = r.json()
    if not isinstance(payload, expect):                    # 3. shape
        raise ValueError(f"expected {expect.__name__}, got "
                         f"{type(payload).__name__}: {str(payload)[:140]}")
    return payload

try:
    payload = get_json(URL, params={...})
except requests.RequestException as e:
    st.error(f"Could not reach the endpoint: {e}")   # network, timeout, 4xx/5xx
    st.stop()
except ValueError as e:
    st.error(f"It answered, but not with what we asked for: {e}")
    st.stop()
```

The two `except` clauses are different failures and deserve different messages:
one means the server is unreachable, the other means it is reachable and
wrong.

### Client app skeleton

```python
# app.py
import streamlit as st, requests, pandas as pd

st.title("API Client")
lat = st.number_input("Latitude", value=38.9)
lon = st.number_input("Longitude", value=-77.0)

if st.button("Fetch"):
    try:
        r = requests.get("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast",
                         params={"latitude": lat, "longitude": lon, "hourly": "temperature_2m"},
                         timeout=10)
        r.raise_for_status()
        h = r.json()["hourly"]
        df = pd.DataFrame({"time": pd.to_datetime(h["time"]), "temp": h["temperature_2m"]})
        st.line_chart(df.set_index("time"))
    except Exception as e:
        st.error(f"Could not fetch data: {e}")
```
